p54.title: Countdown from 30 to 25
p54.statement:
Count from **30** down to **25** and print each number **on its own line**; that is 30, 29, 28, 27, 26, 25.

This problem has no input.
hints: To count backwards, you need the step `-1`.
The end of the range must be 24 so that 25 is inside it.
p54.guideTitle: Countdown from 30 to 25 — range with a negative step
mistakes: Writing `range(30, 25, -1)`: the number 25 is not printed.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range and step -1
steps: We decide the counting range from 30 to 25.
With `range(30, 24, -1)` we take the numbers going down from 30.
We print each number on one line.
explain: `range` with three inputs works as `range(start, stop, step)`. A step of -1 means we subtract one each time. We set the end to 24, because `range` does not include its end and 25 must be printed.
If we had set the end to 25, the number 25 would not be printed. Always check this boundary in a countdown.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with subtracting one
steps: We start the counter from 30.
As long as the counter is greater than or equal to 25, we print it.
In each round we subtract one from the counter.
explain: In a countdown the counter decreases in each round. The condition `i >= 25` is true while we are still at 25 or above; as soon as it becomes smaller than 25, the loop ends.
Both methods have exactly the same output, so the choice between them depends on your taste.

p55.title: Countdown from 10 to 1
p55.statement:
Count backwards from **10** to **1**; each number is printed **on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Set the step to `-1` and the end of the range to `0` (the number zero is not part of the range).
`range(10, 0, -1)` gives exactly this range.
p55.guideTitle: Countdown from 10 to 1 — range with a negative step
mistakes: Forgetting the step `-1`: the loop prints nothing, because going up from 10 to 1 is empty.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range(10, 0, -1)
steps: The counting starts at 10 and continues to 1.
With `range(10, 0, -1)` we take these numbers in reverse order.
We print each number on one line.
explain: The end of the range is zero, because `range` does not include zero, and so 1 is the last number printed.
The step -1 makes `range` come down instead of going up; this method makes the countdown short and readable.

solutions.name: Method 2: while as long as it is greater than or equal to one
steps: We start the counter from 10.
As long as the counter has not become smaller than 1, we print it.
We subtract one from the counter in each round.
explain: The condition `i >= 1` includes the number 1, so the last output is 1. If the condition were `i > 1`, 1 would not be printed.
Subtracting from the counter in each round takes the loop towards its end; if we forget it, the loop becomes endless.

p56.title: Even numbers from 0 to 20
p56.statement:
Print the even numbers **0, 2, 4, …, 20**, **each on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Set the step to 2: `range(0, 21, 2)`.
If you do not write the step, all the numbers are printed, not only the even ones.
mistakes: Writing `range(0, 21)` without the step 2: the odd numbers are printed too.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with step 2
steps: We start at zero and go to 20.
With a step of 2 we take only the even numbers.
We print each number on one line.
explain: `range(0, 21, 2)` means start at zero, go forward 2 at a time and stay before 21. The result: 0, 2, 4 … 20, all of which are even.
We set the end to 21 so that 20 is included. This pattern is useful for any other regular distance too.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with increasing by two
steps: We start the counter at zero.
As long as the counter has not become greater than 20, we print it.
In each round we increase the counter by 2.
explain: By increasing by two in each round, the counter always stays even, because we started from zero. The condition `i <= 20` includes the upper boundary.
If we had increased the counter by one, the odd numbers would have been printed too; choosing the right step builds the right answer.

p57.title: Odd numbers from 1 to 9
p57.statement:
Print the odd numbers **1, 3, 5, 7, 9**, **each on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Set the start to 1 and the step to 2.
The end of the range is 10; since 10 is not part of the range, the last number is 9.
mistakes: Starting from zero: zero is even and must not be printed.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with step 2
steps: We start from one and go to 9.
With a step of 2 we take only the odd numbers.
We print each number on one line.
explain: `range(1, 10, 2)` starts at 1 and with a step of 2 reaches 3, 5, 7 and 9. The end is 10 so that 9 is included, and the number 11 is no longer in the range.
Since the start is odd, with a step of 2 all the numbers stay odd.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with increasing by two
steps: We start the counter from 1.
As long as it has not become greater than 9, we print it.
In each round we add two.
explain: Starting from 1 and adding 2 always gives odd numbers. The condition `i <= 9` includes the last odd number.
This method shows that the pattern "start + step" gives the same result in a `while` loop as in `range`.

p58.title: Countdown to the input number
p58.statement:
Read a natural number `n` (`n ≥ 1`).

Count backwards from `n` to `1` and print each number **on its own line**.
hints: Read `n` with `int(input())`.
Put the step `-1` in `range` and the end `0` (zero is not part of the range).
p58.guideTitle: Countdown to the input number — input and range
mistakes: Forgetting `int`: `input()` gives text and `range` needs a number.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range(n, 0, -1)
steps: We read the number `n` from the input.
With `range(n, 0, -1)` we count backwards from `n` to 1.
We print each number on one line.
explain: We set the start of `range` equal to `n`, so the counting starts from the very number the user entered. The end is zero so that 1 is the last number.
Since `n` comes from the user, the program works for any `n`; that means we put the input number in place of a fixed number.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with the input counter
steps: We read the number `n` and make it the counter.
As long as the counter is greater than or equal to 1, we print it.
In each round we subtract one from the counter.
explain: The number the user enters becomes the counter directly. From then on the counter decreases by one in each round until it reaches 1.
The problem statement gives only natural numbers; so `n` is never less than 1 and the loop runs at least once.

p59.title: Counting from a to b
p59.statement:
Read two integers `a` and `b` (each on its own line); `a ≤ b`.

Print all the numbers from `a` to `b` (including `a` and `b` themselves), **each on its own line**.
hints: The end of `range` must be `b + 1` so that `b` is printed too.
Read `a` and `b` separately with `input()`.
p59.guideTitle: Counting from a to b — two input numbers and range
mistakes: Writing `range(a, b)`: the number `b` is not printed.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range(a, b + 1)
steps: We read the two numbers `a` and `b`, each on its own line.
With `range(a, b + 1)` we make an interval that includes both ends.
We print each number on one line.
explain: Since `range` does not include its end, to get `b` we must write `b + 1`. This is the only change needed to make the closed interval "from a to b".
The case `a = b` works correctly too: the interval has only one number and that number is printed.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with a counter from a
steps: We read the two numbers and start the counter from `a`.
As long as the counter has not become greater than `b`, we print it.
We increase the counter by one in each round.
explain: The condition `i <= b` includes both `a` and `b`, because the counter starts from `a` and continues as long as it has not gone above `b`.
This method builds the same interval with a manual counter. The two methods behave the same at the upper boundary, and this boundary is one of the main points of this problem.

p60.title: Multiplication table of 3
p60.statement:
Print the multiplication table of **3** from `3 x 1` to `3 x 10`. Each row must be exactly in this form:

`3 x 1 = 3`

This problem has no input.
hints: Take a counter from 1 to 10 and in each row print `3` and the counter.
Remember that the product is `3 * i`.
mistakes: Writing `3 * i` without the text `x` and `=`: the output format is not correct.

solutions.name: Method 1: print with several arguments
steps: We make a loop for the factors from 1 to 10.
In each round with `print` we give the parts of the row separately: `3 x`, the factor, `=` and the result.
`print` puts one space between the arguments and the row comes out exactly in the requested form.
explain: When `print` gets several arguments, it puts them side by side with one space. So `print("3 x", i, "=", 3 * i)` prints exactly `3 x 1 = 3`.
`3 * i` calculates the product. We put the letters `x` and `=` inside quotes so that they are printed as text.

solutions.name: Method 2: building the row with + and str
steps: We run the loop from 1 to 10.
With `str` we turn the numbers into text and join them with `+`.
We print the complete row we built once.
explain: `str` turns a number into text, because `+` does not work between a text and a number. If we forget `str`, Python gives a type error.
Building the row in the variable `line` lets us see the format before printing. This method is useful for more complicated formats too.

p61.title: Each letter of a word on one line
p61.statement:
Read one English word (without spaces).

Print each of its letters **on its own line**, from the start of the word to the end.
hints: A string can be read letter by letter with `for`.
The loop variable is itself a letter of the word; print that.
p61.guideTitle: Each letter of the word on a line — going over the letters
mistakes: Printing the whole word in each repeat: each line must be one letter.

solutions.name: Method 1: for over the word itself
steps: We read the word.
With `for ch in word` we take the word letter by letter.
We print each letter on one line with `print`.
explain: A string in Python can be iterated; `for ch in word` gives each letter in order from the start to the end. We do not need to manage the indexes ourselves.
Since the input word has no spaces, each letter is printed exactly once and the order is kept.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with an index
steps: We start the index `i` from zero.
As long as `i` is smaller than the length of the word, we print the letter at place `i`.
In each round we move `i` forward by one.
explain: `word[i]` gives the letter at place `i`. `len(word)` is the length of the word, so the condition `i < len(word)` continues exactly to the last letter.
This method builds the `for` iteration with an index. If we forget to increase the index, the loop becomes endless.

p62.title: Each word of a line on its own line
p62.statement:
Read a line of text; the words are separated by spaces.

Print each word **on its own line**.
hints: `split()` puts the words of a line in a list.
Loop over the list of words with `for`.
p62.guideTitle: Each word of a line on its own line — split and going over
mistakes: Printing the whole line instead of each word: the output must show the words separately.

solutions.name: Method 1: split and for
steps: We read the input line with `input()`.
With `split()` we turn it into a list of words.
We print each word on its own line with `print`.
explain: `split()` without an argument breaks the text at spaces; so `a b c` becomes the list `['a', 'b', 'c']`. `for` takes each word in order and `print` writes it on its own line.
If the line has only one word, `split` gives a list with that one word and the output is correct.

solutions.name: Method 2: the list of words and an index
steps: We read the line and put the list of words in `words`.
With `range(len(words))` we get the indexes.
We print the word at each index.
explain: We build the list `words` once and then go over it with the indexes. `len(words)` gives the number of words and `range` gives the indexes.
This method gives the same output; the only difference is that we reach the words by index, which is more useful in later problems.

p63.title: Counting with step 10 from 0 to 100
p63.statement:
Print the numbers **0, 10, 20, …, 100**, **each on its own line**.

This problem has no input.
hints: Set the step to 10 and the end of the range to 101 (because 101 is not part of the range).
If you set the end to 100, the number 100 is not printed.
mistakes: Writing the end of `range` as 100: the number 100 is not printed.

solutions.name: Method 1: for with range and step 10
steps: We consider the range 0 to 100 with a step of 10.
With `range(0, 101, 10)` we take the numbers.
We print each number on one line.
explain: The end of the range is 101 so that 100 is included. A step of 10 means we go forward ten units each time: 0, 10, 20 … 100.
This method is the same for any other regular step; we only change the step and the boundaries.

solutions.name: Method 2: while with increasing by ten
steps: We start the counter at zero.
As long as it has not gone above 100, we print it.
In each round we add ten.
explain: The condition `i <= 100` includes 100 itself. By adding 10 in each round, the counter always stays a multiple of 10.
Both methods have the same output; `for` with a known range is shorter and `while` is more flexible.
